p1-test-function.text: Imagine you're checking a delivery rule before it goes live. The fee is waived when the order has at least ten items.
Before you touch the code, decide what should happen at exactly ten. That's the value we will come back to.
The first function uses greater than ten. Nine returns false, and eleven returns true. Both answers look fine.
Now try ten. The function returns false. Our rule includes ten, so the expected answer is true.
An assert checks that a condition is true. If it is false, Python stops and tells us which check failed.
Here, the test records our expectation. The failure tells us where to look. It doesn't tell us to change the expectation.
Change greater than to greater than or equal to. Run all three tests, including the ones that already passed.
A boundary test checks the point where the result changes. The neighbouring values help catch a repair that breaks either side.
A parcel is accepted if it weighs at most five kilograms. Which values would catch a function that rejects exactly five?
Pause and write the expected answer for each value. Then explain which of your tests distinguishes the two rules.

dd-quartiles.text: Five requests took twelve, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen and eighteen minutes. Picture them in order, one dot per request.
The middle is the third position. That puts the median at fifteen minutes. There are two positions on either side.
For the mean, add the waits and divide by how many there are. Seventy-five divided by five gives fifteen.
Now imagine the longest request took forty-eight minutes. Pause and predict which number moves, the mean or the median.
The sum rises by thirty minutes. Shared across five requests, that raises the mean by six, from fifteen to twenty-one.
The third position still holds fifteen. The median stays there. One number reports the average cost in minutes. The other locates the middle wait.
For quartiles, leave out the centre of this odd-sized batch and find the median of each half. Twelve and fourteen give thirteen.
The upper half changes from sixteen and eighteen to sixteen and forty-eight. Its median moves from seventeen to thirty-two. The gap between the quartiles grows from four to nineteen.
Try these six waits. Find the middle using both central positions, then split the data into two halves to find the quartiles.
In your handover, say what the typical middle wait was and mention the longest wait separately. Tell the reader how many requests you observed.

mth-sets.text: A team has twenty-four people. Twelve can review code, nine can test releases, and five can do both.
If you add twelve and nine, who gets counted twice? Think about one person who belongs to both groups.
Put the five people who do both in the overlap. Seven people review only, and four test only.
These are disjoint groups. That means no one belongs to two of the three regions we just made.
Seven plus five plus four gives sixteen people who do at least one of the tasks. The other eight do neither.
We can get sixteen another way. Add twelve and nine, then subtract five to undo the extra count of everyone in both groups.
This is more than a shortcut. It gives you a way to audit a report. Every person in the union is also in the whole team.
So if the count you calculate is larger than the team, some of the reported figures cannot be true together.
Try a different report. The team has eighteen people. Twelve review, nine test, and two do both.
Calculate the union, then compare it with the team size. Give both steps in your written argument so another person can check your reasoning.
